title: Seed Calculator for Your Garden 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calculate Seeds Needed for Your Garden
description: Calculate how many seeds you need per square meter for lettuce, tomato, carrot, radish and spinach. Accounts for germination rates and spacing. Free.
intro:
Planning a productive home garden begins long before the first seedling sprouts: you need to know **how many seeds to buy and sow per square meter** for each crop. Buy too few and you end up with bare patches and wasted growing time; sow too many and the seedlings compete for light, water and nutrients — yielding stunted, low-quality plants. This calculator gives you a straightforward estimate of total seeds required based on your **garden area in square meters** and the **crop type** you plan to grow.

The core formula is:

**Seeds Needed = Garden Area (m²) × Recommended Seed Density (seeds/m²) ÷ Expected Germination Rate**

Seed density varies dramatically by species. Carrots, with their tiny seeds and shallow taproots, are typically sown at around **200 seeds per square meter** with later thinning to roughly 80-100 mature plants. Lettuce is sown at **30-40 seeds per m²** then thinned to 16-25 final heads. Tomatoes, which need substantial space and are usually transplanted as seedlings, only require about **3-4 seeds per square meter of final bed** — though you typically start with 6-8 seeds per cell in trays to account for germination failures. Radishes pack tightly at **150-200 seeds per m²** because of their short cycle (25-35 days from sowing to harvest) and small root size. Spinach falls in the middle at **80-100 seeds per m²**.

The second variable is the **germination rate**, which depends on seed freshness, storage conditions and species genetics. Most commercially packaged vegetable seeds advertise 80-90% germination at the time of packaging, but viability declines with each year of storage — and field conditions (soil temperature, moisture, depth of sowing) typically reduce real-world germination to **70-85%**. Sowing 10-30% more seeds than you actually want as mature plants compensates for this gap. After germination you **thin** the seedlings to the final spacing recommended for each crop.

This calculator returns the total number of seeds you should purchase or set aside for direct sowing. It assumes standard horticultural practices for temperate climates and is intended for hobby home gardeners, school gardens and small market-garden plots up to 100 m². For commercial operations, certified organic farms, or specialty seed varieties, consult your local **USDA Cooperative Extension Service**, university agricultural extension program or a professional agronomist for site-specific guidance.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **seeds_needed = area_m2 × species_density**. Enter your garden area and select your crop. The calculator provides the exact number of seeds you'll need to account for typical germination rates (70-85%).
useCases: Planning a 10 m² backyard lettuce bed: at 30 seeds/m² you need 300 seeds, plus 15% buffer for germination = roughly 345 seeds — about three small commercial packets.
Starting a 4 m² carrot patch for fall harvest: 200 seeds/m² × 4 m² = 800 seeds, which is about one standard packet (1,000 seeds at $5-8 USD retail price).
Setting up a 6 m² tomato bed with seedling transplants: 4 plants/m² × 6 m² = 24 final plants, so sow 48-60 seeds in trays (2-3 per cell) to allow for germination failure and thinning.
Building a community garden with twelve 3 m² mixed-vegetable plots: total area 36 m², plan for ~7,200 carrot seeds, 1,080 lettuce seeds, 144 tomato seeds and 5,400 radish seeds across rotation.
Stretching a tight gardening budget by sizing seed orders precisely instead of buying excess packets that lose viability after 2-3 years of storage.
Teaching elementary-school students about garden math by computing seed requirements for a 5 m² school plot — practical hands-on application of multiplication and percentages.
Planning succession sowing of radishes every 14 days in a 2 m² strip to ensure continuous harvest May-October: each sowing needs about 300-400 seeds.
Estimating seed inventory for a small market garden producing baby-leaf spinach: 50 m² at 100 seeds/m² with 80% germination = ~6,250 seeds per cycle, planned across the season.

## How the calculation works

This calculator multiplies your available garden area by the seed density requirement for your chosen crop. It accounts for typical germination rates and spacing recommendations, helping you purchase the right amount of seeds for successful germination and plant spacing.

## Important notes

This calculator provides guidance based on standard horticultural practices. For critical decisions (commercial operations, unique growing conditions), consult with local agricultural extension services or a professional agronomist. Data is current as of 2026 and reviewed periodically for accuracy.

faq.q: How does the calculator determine the seed density per square meter?
faq.a: The calculator uses widely accepted horticultural guidelines for each crop's optimal **plant spacing** and final density, then adjusts upward to compensate for typical germination rates of 70-85% under field conditions. For carrots, the recommended in-row spacing is roughly 3-5 cm with rows 20-30 cm apart, yielding approximately 200 seeds sown per square meter (later thinned to 80-100 mature roots). Lettuce is sown at 30-40 seeds/m² for head varieties (final spacing 25-30 cm) or 80-100 seeds/m² for baby-leaf cut-and-come-again production. Tomatoes occupy 3-4 plants/m² in a final bed at 50-60 cm spacing. These figures align with USDA Cooperative Extension Service recommendations and the Royal Horticultural Society growing guides, with minor variations between varieties.

faq.q: Should I direct-sow seeds or start them indoors as transplants?
faq.a: It depends on the crop and your climate. **Direct sowing** works best for crops with sensitive taproots that resent transplanting — carrots, radishes, parsnips and most root vegetables fall into this category. **Indoor starts (transplants)** are essential for warm-season crops like tomatoes, peppers and eggplants in temperate climates where the outdoor season is too short to direct-sow; you start them 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant when soil temperatures exceed 15°C (60°F). **Either approach** works for lettuce, spinach, kale, and most brassicas — direct sowing is cheaper and simpler, while transplants give you a 4-6 week head start on the season. The calculator estimates total seeds required regardless of method, but if you use transplants you typically sow 2-3 seeds per cell and thin to the strongest, which reduces total seed consumption.

faq.q: What is the best planting time for each crop?
faq.a: Planting time depends on your **USDA Hardiness Zone**, frost dates and the specific crop's temperature requirements. **Cool-season crops** (lettuce, spinach, peas, radishes, kale) prefer soil temperatures of 7-21°C (45-70°F) and tolerate light frost — sow in early spring (March-April in temperate northern hemisphere) or late summer-early fall (August-September) for a fall harvest. **Warm-season crops** (tomatoes, peppers, beans, cucumbers, squash) need soil temperatures above 15°C (60°F) and zero frost — direct-sow or transplant after your average last spring frost date, typically May-June in temperate zones. **Carrots** are unusual: they tolerate cool weather but the seeds germinate slowly in cold soil, so wait until soil reaches at least 10°C (50°F). Check your local extension service for region-specific planting calendars.

faq.q: Can I save seeds from my own harvest for next season?
faq.a: Yes, and many home gardeners do it routinely to save money and preserve heirloom varieties. The success rate depends on the **type of seed**: **open-pollinated and heirloom varieties** breed true — saving seeds from healthy parent plants yields offspring identical to the original. **F1 hybrid varieties** (common in commercial seed catalogs) do *not* breed true — saved F2 seeds produce unpredictable, often disappointing offspring. The general procedure is to let one or two of your healthiest plants flower and mature to seed (most crops bolt in summer or fall), collect the seeds, dry them thoroughly at room temperature, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dark place. Properly stored, lettuce and tomato seeds remain viable for 4-6 years; carrot and onion seeds are shorter-lived (1-2 years). Always label with crop, variety and harvest date.

faq.q: Are organic seeds worth the extra cost?
faq.a: Organic seeds are produced from parent plants grown without synthetic pesticides, herbicides or chemical fertilizers and are certified under standards like USDA Organic or EU Organic. They typically cost 30-100% more than conventional seeds. **Benefits**: complete control over chemical exposure (relevant if you garden organically yourself), support for organic-seed breeding programs, and slightly better adaptation to lower-input growing systems. **Drawbacks**: higher price, sometimes lower availability of specific varieties, and germination rates that may be marginally lower than conventional seeds. For most **home gardeners**, the practical difference in harvest quality between organic and conventional seeds is small — both will grow well in healthy soil. Buy organic if it matches your values and budget; otherwise conventional seeds are perfectly adequate.

faq.q: How accurate are these seed estimates for my specific climate?
faq.a: The estimates are based on **standard horticultural practices for temperate climates** and represent solid averages, but actual results vary by 20-40% depending on soil quality, weather patterns, watering consistency, pest pressure and the specific seed variety. If you garden in extreme conditions (very short growing season, very hot tropical climate, sandy or heavy clay soil) you should adjust: hotter climates often require denser sowing for cool-season crops because of faster bolt; sandy soils with poor water retention may need denser sowing of small-seeded crops to ensure adequate germination. For commercial or serious market-garden operations, **consult your local Cooperative Extension Service** (in the US) or equivalent national agricultural research body — they publish detailed crop-by-crop recommendations calibrated to your specific region and soil type.

faq.q: How deep should I plant each type of seed?
faq.a: The general rule of thumb is to **plant seeds at a depth of 2-3 times their diameter**. Tiny seeds like carrots, lettuce, and spinach should be planted very shallowly (about 0.5 cm or 1/4 inch) or simply scattered on top of fine soil and pressed in gently. Radish seeds, slightly larger, go at about 1 cm (1/2 inch). Tomato seeds in starter trays are typically planted at 0.5-1 cm (1/4-1/2 inch). **Planting too deep** is the #1 cause of poor germination for small-seeded crops — the seedling exhausts its energy before reaching sunlight. **Planting too shallow** risks the seed drying out before germination. Keep the seedbed consistently moist until seedlings emerge (typically 7-14 days for most vegetables) by misting daily or covering with a thin layer of damp burlap.

faq.q: What is thinning and when should I do it?
faq.a: **Thinning** is the practice of removing excess seedlings after germination so that the remaining plants have adequate space to develop. Because gardeners sow more seeds than they want final plants (to compensate for germination failures), thinning is almost always necessary. For carrots, thin to the recommended in-row spacing (3-5 cm) when seedlings are 2-3 cm tall and have their first true leaves — typically 2-3 weeks after germination. Lettuce is thinned to 25-30 cm for head varieties at about 4-5 weeks. **Method**: use small scissors to cut excess seedlings at soil level rather than pulling them, which disturbs the roots of the keepers you want to retain. The thinnings of lettuce, spinach, beet greens and carrot tops are perfectly edible and make a delicious addition to salads — nothing is wasted.

faq.q: How long do unused seeds remain viable?
faq.a: Seed viability varies widely by species and storage conditions. Stored in a **cool, dry, dark place** (ideally 5-15°C with low humidity), approximate viability is: **lettuce, tomato, radish, brassicas**: 4-6 years; **spinach, beet, peas, beans**: 3-4 years; **carrot, parsley, parsnip**: 1-3 years; **onion, leek, sweet corn**: 1-2 years (the shortest-lived). To **test old seeds**, sprout 10 seeds on a damp paper towel inside a sealed bag at room temperature for 7-10 days, then count how many germinate. If 7 of 10 sprout, you have 70% viability and should sow more thickly to compensate. Sealed in airtight containers with silica gel desiccant in a refrigerator, viability can be extended substantially beyond these ranges.

faq.q: Is this seed calculator suitable for raised beds or container gardens?
faq.a: Yes, the seed-per-square-meter density values apply equally to raised beds, in-ground plots and large containers — what matters is the **available planting area**, not whether it's framed with timber, sits on legs, or is on a balcony. For containers smaller than 0.5 m² (typical patio pots), the calculator will return small numbers that are easier to plan by hand: a 30 cm × 30 cm pot (0.09 m²) needs only about 3 lettuce seeds or 18 carrot seeds. For **vertical or square-foot gardening** systems, the underlying density assumptions still apply — translate the square-foot grid spacing to seeds per m² for input. Bear in mind that container gardens often require slightly closer spacing than ground beds because of more uniform water and nutrient delivery.

faq.q: Does the calculator save my data or require an account?
faq.a: No. All calculations happen entirely in your browser using client-side JavaScript — your garden area, crop selection and resulting seed count never leave your device. No data is sent to our servers, no cookies are required to perform the calculation, and you do not need to register or log in. This is consistent with our overall privacy approach across every calculator on the site: results are computed locally, instantly and anonymously. If you want to preserve your garden plan across sessions, simply note the results in a spreadsheet or your garden journal — the calculator will produce the same numbers any time you re-enter the inputs.
